newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan discreetly props up its banks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan discreetly props up its banks.

text.p: Japan's monetary authorities, claiming that the worst is over for the nation's financial crisis, is still propping up the fragile banking system discreetly to keep global concerns from flaring up again.
The Ministry of Finance (MOF) appears to be parking a substantial volume of dollar-denominated deposits, using cash raised through dollar buying intervention, at commercial banks.
This helps banks to operate in international financial markets without problems by ensuring ample dollar cash in hand, banking sources said.

A year ago, a series of fiascoes at Japanese financial institutions, including Daiwa Bank's huge losses in unauthorised bond trading in New York, raised global concerns about the Japanese financial system.

This resulted in a "Japan premium" which Japanese banks are asked to pay as an additional cost in borrowing funds overseas, making it virtually impossible for some banks to raise funds in the offshore markets.

The premium has been around 10 basis points for major Japanese banks recently after being pushed up to 50 basis or The sources said the continuing aid from the MOF in the form of dollar deposits is helping to cap possible rises in the Japan premium, which might otherwise resurface.
"MOF deposits are still running, although the overall volume may be declining," said one bank official.
A MOF official said he was aware of the deposits, which had existed for some time, but declined to comment on whether they were designed to help deal with fund-raising problems at specific banks.
"We are aware of it merely as a means to diversify management of external assets (of the Government)," he said.
Japan's external reserves, the world's largest, have increased sharply in the past year and a half. They stood at $214.03 billion at end-August from $125.94 billion at end-February 1995.

Banking sources said the rise in foreign assets was largely due to a heavy volume of currency intervention last year to stem the yen's sharp rise, which sent the dollar down to a post-war record low of 79.75 yen in April.

The sources said the MOF does not directly channel funds to troubled banks but does it through banks with high credit ratings, to make transactions in the money market look natural to those not involved in the deals.
A halt in support by the MOF could cause problems to many banks in which a failure of one bank may risk spilling over into the overall banking system, analysts said.

"The situation surrounding the banking system in Japan does not warrant a quick withdrawl of deposits from commercial banks," said Testufumi Yamakawa, vice president and director of Japan economic research at Goldman Sachs (Japan) Ltd.
"Given negative views by overseas operators and risks that their concerns flare up again, it would be safe to maintain ample liquidities (at some banks)," he added.
Shinano Morita, a director at Standard & Poor's in Tokyo said: "Without support by the government (in various aspects), it may not be strange if the Japan premium resumes rising".
She said the banking system is still vulnerable despite steps taken by banks and the government in the past year, with no quick improvement in sight.

In June, parliament passed bills to clean up the nation's bad loan mess and deal with bank failures, coupled with a scheme to wind up failed mortgage firms using taxpayers' money. Japan's 21 largest banks' disposed of about 10.7 trillion yen of loan losses at the end of March.
Anlaysts and economists said the presence of Japanese banks in the international markets is likely to fall.
Unlike Western banks, many Japanese banks customarily raise short-term funds on offshore markets to make long-term lending to corporations.
But rises in funding costs on short-term borrowing and the Japan premium make it difficult to reap profits in their international lending business.
"Japanese banks' behaviour, different from international standards, is now in the process of being rectified," said Masayuki Kichikawa, an economist at Nomura Research Institute.

Taisuke Tanaka, market strategist at Credit Suisse in Tokyo, said the MOF's deposits might be aimed at allowing some ailing banks to gradually withdraw from their international business without serious damage.
